opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a useful comparison, though you have to be careful about what you're counting.

The human genome is roughly three billion base pairs. That's something like 750 megabytes of raw information, and most of it isn't doing anything especially clever. A lot is repetitive or non-functional. If you ask how much of it plausibly specifies the brain's learning machinery, the architecture, the developmental program, the reward circuitry, the innate priors, you probably land somewhere in the tens of megabytes at most. Maybe less. So the "algorithm" evolution handed us is not some astronomically complex object. It fits in a pretty small file.

On the other side, the code that defines and trains GPT-4 is, if anything, much smaller. The transformer architecture, the optimizer, the training loop, the data pipeline: you can write the core of that in a few thousand lines. Even with all the engineering details, infrastructure, and tricks, the description length of the learning algorithm itself is tiny compared to the genome. Almost all of GPT-4's complexity lives in the weights, and the weights come from the data, not from the algorithm.

So I think the takeaway is that neither system gets most of its competence from a really intricate hand-specified algorithm. In both cases you have a relatively compact learning procedure, and the sophistication comes from running it on a huge amount of experience. For humans, that's a lifetime of sensory data plus whatever evolution baked in. For GPT-4, it's trillions of tokens of text.

Where the comparison gets interesting is the priors. Evolution had an enormous amount of compute, billions of years of selection, to find a small genome that encodes really good inductive biases. Things like how to learn quickly from little data, what to pay attention to, how to structure motivation. Humans are dramatically more sample-efficient than current models. A child learns language from maybe tens of millions of words; GPT-4 sees orders of magnitude more. So evolution might have compressed something genuinely valuable into those megabytes, and we're compensating for not having it by throwing more data and compute at the problem.

That's part of why I don't think the small size of the genome tells you that human-level AI is easy, but it does tell you there probably isn't some vast amount of hidden complexity you'd need to reproduce. The gap looks more like "find better priors and more efficient learning," or just "scale until it doesn't matter," rather than "replicate an incomprehensibly complex design." And that has pretty direct implications for timelines.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the genome is roughly 750 MB and that GPT-4’s learning algorithm is tiny by comparison, directly conveying that the genome has far more capacity than the algorithm requires.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the raw numbers are actually kind of interesting here. The human genome is something like 3 billion base pairs, so on the order of a gigabyte of information, and a lot of that is either not doing much or is doing things that have nothing to do with the brain. If you ask how much of it is specifying the learning algorithm that a human brain runs, the honest answer is nobody knows, but it's plausibly a pretty small fraction, maybe tens of megabytes, maybe a lot less.

And then the learning algorithm for GPT-4, if you strip away all the engineering around it, is really not that much. The core ideas fit in a few pages. Transformers, Adam, a particular initialization, a particular learning rate schedule, some data filtering heuristics. You could write the whole thing down in a few thousand lines of code, and the parts that really matter are a lot smaller than that. So in terms of raw description length, the ML algorithm is almost certainly much simpler than whatever evolution encoded.

But I think that comparison is a little misleading in both directions. On one hand, the genome doesn't have to encode the learning algorithm from scratch in the way a program does. It gets to lean on a lot of physics and chemistry and developmental biology, so the effective description is doing a lot of work that isn't visible if you just count base pairs. On the other hand, the genome has had a huge amount of optimization pressure applied to it over hundreds of millions of years, and most of what it's encoding is not clever learning tricks, it's things like which neurons connect to which, what the reward signals are, a bunch of inductive biases about faces and language and social behavior that get the learner off the ground quickly.

The thing I find most striking is that the ML side, with much less prior knowledge baked in, gets to make up the difference with vastly more data and compute than a human child ever sees. A human sees maybe a few hundred million words in their lifetime, GPT-4 sees orders of magnitude more. So I tend to read the comparison as evidence that you don't need a very complicated learning algorithm to get general intelligence. Evolution found something fairly simple plus a lot of priors, and we found something even simpler plus a lot of data. And that makes me think the remaining gap between these systems and humans is less about discovering some deep algorithmic secret and more about scale and the right kind of experience, which is both encouraging and a little alarming depending on your perspective.

r001.rationale: It describes the genome as roughly a gigabyte of information and GPT-4’s core learning algorithm as only a few pages or a few thousand lines, communicating that the genome has far more capacity than the algorithm requires.

astra-6.text:
I think the relevant comparison is between the genome and the code for the learning algorithm, rather than between the genome and all the weights of GPT-4. Most of the information in a human brain comes from learning, just as most of the information in GPT-4’s weights comes from training.

The genome has room for a lot more information than the code describing a typical machine learning algorithm. But it’s doing many other things: it has to specify how to build a body, how cells work, and so on. It’s quite unclear how much of that information is devoted to specifying the learning algorithm, and how much of that is actually essential to intelligence.

So I think it leaves open the possibility that evolution has built in a bunch of useful machinery that we’re missing. But you shouldn’t imagine that the genome is specifying everything a human knows. It’s specifying a process that, when exposed to the right environment, learns those things. And that process could turn out to have a relatively short description, even if the particular implementation evolution found is very complicated.

r001.rationale: The response says the genome has room for “a lot more information” than the code for a typical machine learning algorithm, and frames that comparison as the genome versus GPT-4’s learning algorithm rather than its weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the genome can hold a lot more information than the learning algorithm used to train GPT-4. The genome is on the order of a billion bytes, and even if you discount most of that, you still have room for a pretty complicated program. The basic algorithm we use to train a language model is much more compact than that.

But you have to be careful about what you’re comparing. The weights of GPT-4 contain much more information than its learning algorithm. And similarly, a human brain contains much more information than the genome, because you learn an enormous amount during your life. The genome doesn’t have to specify everything you know. It specifies a process that builds a brain and causes it to learn.

So I don’t think there’s an information-capacity objection to evolution having found a learning algorithm that’s substantially more sophisticated than the one we use for language models. That doesn’t tell you how much of the genome is actually devoted to learning, or how important that sophistication is. But there’s certainly enough room for a lot of machinery that we haven’t figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the genome holds “a lot more information” than GPT-4’s learning algorithm, describes the algorithm as much more compact, and says the genome has room for a complicated program.
